newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTH AFRICAN TAX AMNESTY COMES UNDER FIRE.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH AFRICAN TAX AMNESTY COMES UNDER FIRE.

text.p: The government's new tax amnesty came under fire on Monday for allowing criminals to benefit from the relief of tax, interest and penalties.

The amnesty, due to come into effect on November 1 until the end of February, would also hamper investigations by the Attorney-General's office into drug lords and smugglers benefitting financially from crime, senior State Advocate Willie Viljoen told the parliamentary finance committee.
Viljoen said the amnesty could have major implications for the state's new drive to crack down on crime.
"Our concern is that the proceeds of crime is included in the tax amnesty and we are concerned about the morality of such an amnesty," he said.
In one case, the state stood to forfeit five million rand through the amnesty.
The amnesty had also "prejudiced a new approach that we have...to the fighting of organised crime.
"We have learnt over the years that tackling organised crime merely by means of prosecution for specific offences did not have much success," Viljoen said.
As a result, the state was hitting criminals where it hurt most by attaching their property and money.

The Attorney-General's office provided revenue officials with the information they needed to attach the property of tax evaders and then prosecuted them for tax evasion as well as, for example, drug running.

Viljoen suggested that the proposed legislation on the amnesty should be amended "to indicate that the relief should not apply to the proceeds of crime and should not apply to people who are currently under investigation for tax evasion or any other ciminal investigation."

South African Revenue Services deputy commissioner Kosie Louw said that receiver of revenue could not penalise people for offences committed outside the scope of the Income Tax Act, "be it for illicit diamond dealing or drug smuggling."
